content: Umbilical cord prolapse is a critical obstetric emergency that occurs during pregnancy or labor, posing a significant risk to the fetus's life. This condition arises when the umbilical cord descends outside the uterus while the fetus remains inside. It often happens after the rupture of membranes, where the force of the amniotic fluid expulsion carries the cord along. Once the fetus's presenting part, typically the head, engages in the pelvis, it can compress the cord, cutting off oxygen supply. This can result in fetal brain damage or stillbirth if not addressed immediately. To prevent such outcomes, the baby must be delivered urgently via cesarean section. While awaiting surgical delivery, the mother is positioned in a knee-elbow posture to reduce pressure on the cord. Additionally, a healthcare provider may manually push the presenting fetal part, such as the head, back into the pelvis to prevent cord compression. It is ineffective to attempt to push the cord itself back into the uterus. Another intervention involves infusing 500 mL of fluid into the mother’s bladder via a catheter to elevate the presenting part and alleviate pressure on the prolapsed cord. Several factors increase the risk of umbilical cord prolapse. These include premature rupture of membranes, polyhydramnios (excessive amniotic fluid), and a long umbilical cord. These conditions can facilitate the cord's descent during the rupture of membranes. The prognosis for umbilical cord prolapse varies. In hospital settings or environments with rapid access to emergency care, fetal mortality rates range from 11% to 17%. However, innovative interventions, such as bladder infusion to displace the presenting part, have shown promise in reducing mortality. In one reported series of 24 cases, no fetal deaths occurred when this technique was employed. Certain medications, such as oxytocin, are absolutely contraindicated in cases of umbilical cord prolapse, as they can exacerbate the condition by increasing uterine contractions and further compressing the cord. In some cases, practitioners may attempt immediate vaginal delivery while minimizing pressure on the cord. However, these efforts often fail, necessitating an emergency cesarean section. During preparation for surgery, the mother is placed in the Trendelenburg or knee-elbow position, and a healthcare provider manually displaces the presenting part out of the pelvic inlet to relieve cord compression. If delivery is delayed, the fetus's oxygen and blood supply may be completely occluded, leading to brain damage or death.
